topic: The Fractal Path: Ternary Logic and the Constrained Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: University students (Computer Science/Mathematics) or advanced high school students

outline.topic: The Fractal Path: Ternary Logic and the Constrained Towers of Hanoi
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science/Mathematics) or advanced high school students

sections.title: Introduction: The Restricted Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce the standard Towers of Hanoi but add a 'linear' constraint: disks can only move between adjacent pegs (A ↔ B and B ↔ C). A jump from A to C is forbidden. This restriction transforms a simple puzzle into a complex journey.
sections.example: A curious robot named 'Tertio' is trying to move 3 disks from Peg A to Peg C, but its mechanical arm is stuck—it can only shift disks to the peg immediately to its left or right.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Base-3 (Ternary) Counting
sections.content: Explain ternary counting (Base-3) where digits are 0, 1, and 2. Use a visual 'odometer' representation to show how numbers increment. Emphasize that while binary (Base-2) represents a 'yes/no' state, ternary represents 'left/middle/right' positions.
sections.example: Visualizing the number 13 in ternary: 111 (1*9 + 1*3 + 1*1). In our puzzle, each digit represents the peg location (0=A, 1=B, 2=C) of a specific disk.

sections.title: Mapping States to Ternary Coordinates
sections.content: Assign every possible configuration of the puzzle to a ternary number. For N disks, there are 3^N possible states. The largest disk is the most significant digit, and the smallest disk is the least significant digit.
sections.example: With 2 disks, state '02' means the large disk is on Peg A (0) and the small disk is on Peg C (2). This creates a unique 'address' for every possible layout of the game.

sections.title: The Geometry of Moves: The Sierpinski Gasket
sections.content: Visualize the state space as a graph. Each valid move between states is an edge. Because of the linear constraint, the state-transition graph forms a perfect Sierpinski Triangle (fractal). Moving one disk corresponds to moving along an edge of the triangle.
sections.example: An animation shows that for 1 disk, the graph is a line (A-B-C). For 2 disks, it becomes three connected lines forming a triangle. For 3 disks, it becomes the classic Sierpinski Gasket with 27 vertices.

sections.title: Graph Traversal: Finding the Optimal Path
sections.content: Explain that solving the puzzle is equivalent to traversing the 'outer edge' of the Sierpinski triangle. To get from state 000 (all on Peg A) to 222 (all on Peg C), the robot must visit every single node on the perimeter of the fractal.
sections.example: Trace a glowing line following the perimeter of the Sierpinski triangle. The sequence of nodes visited matches the sequence of ternary numbers if we follow a 'Gray Code' style path for the constrained puzzle.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Beauty of Mathematical Convergence
sections.content: Summarize how ternary counting (number theory), the Towers of Hanoi (algorithms), and the Sierpinski Triangle (fractal geometry) are actually three different ways of looking at the same underlying structure.
sections.example: Zoom out from the small 3-disk triangle to a massive 10-disk Sierpinski fractal, showing how the robot's simple rules create a complex, infinite geometric pattern.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Restricted Puzzle
lecture_lines: Meet the standard Towers of Hanoi puzzle.
But here, disks only move to adjacent pegs.
Jumping from A to C is strictly forbidden.
animations: FadeIn three vertical pegs labeled A, B, and C (#FFFFFF) and 3 disks on Peg A (#FF5733, #33FF57, #3357FF).
Draw a red cross (#FF0000) over a dashed curved arrow between Peg A and Peg C.
Display green double-headed arrows (#00FF00) between Pegs A-B and Pegs B-C.
Animate the smallest disk (#3357FF) sliding from Peg A to Peg B, then from Peg B to Peg C.
Flash the three disks on Peg C and highlight the start (A) and end (C) pegs.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Base-3 (Ternary) Counting
lecture_lines: Counting usually happens in binary or decimal.
Ternary uses digits zero, one, and two.
Think of an odometer with three possible states.
Each digit represents a peg: A, B, or C.
One-one-one in ternary equals thirteen in decimal.
animations: Display a 3-digit ternary counter '000' where each digit represents a disk position.
Animate the counter incrementing through 000, 001, 002, 010 (Base-3) with shifting digits.
Transform digits into peg labels: 0=A (#FFFFFF), 1=B (#87CEEB), 2=C (#90EE90).

storyboard.title: Mapping States to Ternary Coordinates
lecture_lines: Every disk configuration has a unique ternary address.
Largest disks are the most significant digits.
Smallest disks represent the least significant digits.
State 'zero-two' means big on A, small on C.
Three disks create twenty-seven unique state addresses.
animations: Show a configuration: large disk on Peg A (0) and small disk on Peg C (2).
Write the ternary address '02' below the pegs, highlighting digits corresponding to disks.
Display a 3x3 grid of all 9 possible ternary states for two disks (00 to 22).

storyboard.title: The Geometry of Moves: The Sierpinski Gasket
lecture_lines: Valid moves connect states into a geometric graph.
The restricted rule creates a linear state path.
One disk forms a simple three-node line.
Two disks form three lines in a triangle.
Three disks generate the intricate Sierpinski Gasket fractal.
animations: Draw a 3-node horizontal graph (0-1-2) representing valid moves for one disk.
Replicate the line three times and connect the tips into a triangle for two disks.
Show the 9-vertex state graph where each edge is a valid disk move.
Assemble three 2-disk triangles into a larger triangle to represent three disks.
Highlight the final 27-vertex Sierpinski Gasket fractal representing the entire state space.

storyboard.title: Graph Traversal: Finding the Optimal Path
lecture_lines: Solving means traversing the fractal's outer perimeter.
We move from state 'zero-zero-zero' to 'two-two-two'.
This path visits every single vertex on the edge.
animations: Focus on the 3-disk Sierpinski Gasket and label the starting corner state 000.
Trace a glowing gold path (#FFD700) along the outer perimeter of the fractal.
Animate a moving point traveling from 000 through the middle and then to 222.
Flash each vertex on the perimeter as the path visits it in sequence.
Show that solving the puzzle requires visiting every node on the fractal boundary.

storyboard.title: Conclusion: The Beauty of Mathematical Convergence
lecture_lines: Ternary logic and fractals reveal the same truth.
Simple rules build infinite, self-similar geometric patterns.
The constrained puzzle unifies counting, graphs, and geometry.
animations: Overlay ternary strings onto the vertices of the Sierpinski Gasket graph.
Zoom out the camera to reveal a higher-order Sierpinski Gasket (N=6).
Display the title 'The Fractal Path: Ternary Logic' in a glowing gradient (#FFD700).
